A refined version of the Siegel-Shidlovskii theorem

F.Beukers
Abstract

Using Y.André’s result on differential equations satisfied by EE-functions, we derive an improved version of the Siegel-Shidlovskii theorem. It gives a complete characterisation of algebraic relations over the algebraic numbers between values of EE-functions at any non-zero algebraic point.

1 Introduction

In this paper we consider EE-functions. An entire function f⁡(z)f(z) is called an EE-function if it has a powerseries expansion of the form

f⁡(z)=∑k=0∞akk!​zkf(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}{a_{k}\over k!}z^{k}

where

  1. 1.

    ak∈ℚ¯a_{k}\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}} for all kk.

  2. 2.

    h⁡(a0,a1,…,ak)=O⁡(k)h(a_{0},a_{1},\ldots,a_{k})=O(k) for all kk where hh denotes the log of the absolute height.

  3. 3.

    ff satisfies a linear differential equation L​y=0Ly=0 with coefficients in ℚ¯​[z]\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[z].

The linear differential equation L​y=0Ly=0 of minimal order which is satisfied by ff is called the minimal differential equation of ff.

Furthermore, in all of our consideration we take a fixed embedding ℚ¯→ℂ\overline{\mathbb{Q}}\to{\mathbb{C}}.

Siegel first introduced EE-functions around 1929 in his work on transcendence of values of Bessel-functions and related functions. Actually, Siegel’s definition was slightly more general in that condition (3) reads h⁡(a0,a1,…,ak)=o⁡(k​log⁡k)h(a_{0},a_{1},\ldots,a_{k})=o(k\log k). But until now no EE-functions in Siegel’s original definition are known which fail to satisfy condition (2) above. Around 1955 Shidlovski managed to remove Siegel’s technical normality conditions and we now have the following theorem (see [Sh, Chapter 4.4],[FN, Theorem 5.23]).

Theorem 1.1 (Siegel-Shidlovskii, 1956)

Let f1,…,fnf_{1},\ldots,f_{n} be a set of EE-functions which satisfy the system of first order equations

dd​z​(y1yn)=A​(y1yn){d\over dz}\pmatrix{y_{1}\cr\vdots\cr y_{n}\cr}=A\pmatrix{y_{1}\cr\vdots\cr y_{n}\cr}

where AA is an n×nn\times n-matrix with entries in ℚ¯​(z)\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(z). Denote the common denominator of the entries of AA by T⁡(z)T(z). Then, for any ξ∈ℚ¯\xi\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}} such that ξ​T​(ξ)≠0\xi T(\xi)\neq 0 we have

degtrℚ¯​(f1​(ξ),…,fn​(ξ))=degtrℚ¯​(z)​(f1​(z),…,fn​(z)).{\rm degtr}_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}}(f_{1}(\xi),\ldots,f_{n}(\xi))={\rm degtr}_{\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(z)}(f_{1}(z),\ldots,f_{n}(z)).

In [B1] Daniel Bertrand gives an alternative proof of the Siegel-Shidlovskii theorem using Laurent’s determinants.

Using the Siegel-Shidlovskii Theorem it is possible to prove the following theorem.

Of course the Siegel-Shidlovskii theorem suggests strongly that all relations between values of EE-functions at algebraic points arise by specialisation of polynomial relations over ℚ¯​(z)\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(z). Using the techniques of the Siegel-Shidlovskii techniques this turns out to be true up to a finite exceptional set of algebraic points.

Theorem 1.2 (Nesterenko-Shidlovskii, 1996)

There exists a finite set SS such that for all ξ∈ℚ¯,ξ∉S\xi\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}},\xi\not\in S the following holds. For any homogeneous polynomial relation P⁡(f1​(ξ),…,fn​(ξ))=0P(f_{1}(\xi),\ldots,f_{n}(\xi))=0 with P∈ℚ¯​[X1,…,Xn]P\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}] there exists Q∈ℚ¯​[z,X1,…,Xn]Q\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[z,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}], homogeneous in XiX_{i}, such that Q⁡(z,f1​(z),…,fn​(z))≡0Q(z,f_{1}(z),\ldots,f_{n}(z))\equiv 0 and P⁡(X1,…,Xn)=Q⁡(ξ,X1,…,Xn)P(X_{1},\ldots,X_{n})=Q(\xi,X_{1},\ldots,X_{n}).

In the statement of the Theorem one can drop the word ‘homogeneous’ if one wants, simply by considering the set of EE-functions 1,f1​(z),…,fn​(z)1,f_{1}(z),\ldots,f_{n}(z) instead. Loosely speaking, for almost all ξ∈ℚ¯\xi\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}, polynomial relations between the values of fif_{i} at z=ξz=\xi arise by specialisation of polynomial relations between the fi​(z)f_{i}(z) over ℚ¯​(z)\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(z).

In [NS] it is also remarked that the exceptional set SS can be computed in principle. Although Theorem 1.2 is not stated explicitly in [NS], it is immediate from Theorem 1 and Lemmas 1,2 in [NS].

Around 1997 Y.André (see [A1] and Theorem 2.1 below) discovered that the nature of differential equations satisfied by EE-functions is very simple. Their only non-trivial singularities are at 0,∞0,\infty. Even more astounding is that this observation allowed André to prove transcendence statements, as illustrated in Theorem 2.2. In particular André managed to give a completely new proof of the Siegel-Shidlovskii Theorem using his discovery. In order to achieve this, a defect relation for linear equations with irregular singularities had to be invoked. For a survey one can consult [A2] or, more detailed, [B2].

However, it turns out that even more is possible. Theorem 2.1 allows us to prove the following Theorem.

Theorem 1.3

Theorem 1.2 holds for any ξ∈ℚ¯\xi\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}} with ξ​T​(ξ)≠0\xi T(\xi)\neq 0.

The proof of this Theorem will be given in section 3, after the necessary preparations. In particular we will use some very basic facts about differential galois groups of systems of differential equations. All that we require is contained in Section 1.4 of the book [PS].

One particular consequence of Theorem 1.3 is the solution of Conjecture A in [NS].

Corollary 1.4

Let assumption be as in Theorem 1.1. Suppose that f1​(z),…,fn​(z)f_{1}(z),\ldots,f_{n}(z) are linearly independent over ℚ¯​(z)\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(z). Then for any ξ∈ℚ¯\xi\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}, with ξ​T​(ξ)≠0\xi T(\xi)\neq 0, the numbers f1​(ξ),…,fn​(ξ)f_{1}(\xi),\ldots,f_{n}(\xi) are ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}}-linear independent.

A question that remains is about the nature of relations between values of EE-functions at singular points ≠0\neq 0. The best known example is f⁡(z)=(z−1)​ezf(z)=(z-1)e^{z}. Its differential equation has a singularity at z=1z=1 and it vanishes at z=1z=1, even though f⁡(z)f(z) is transcendental over ℚ¯​(z)\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(z). Of course the vanishing of f⁡(z)f(z) at z=1z=1 arises in a trivial way and one would probably agree that it is better to look at eze^{z} itself. It turns out that all relations between values of EE-functions at singularities ≠0\neq 0 arise in a similar trivial fashion. This is a consequence of the following Theorem.

Theorem 1.5

Let f1,…,fnf_{1},\ldots,f_{n} be as above and suppose they are ℚ¯​(z)\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(z)-linear independent. Then there exist EE-functions e1​(z),…,en​(z)e_{1}(z),\ldots,e_{n}(z) and an n×nn\times n-matrix MM with entries in ℚ¯​[z]\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[z] such that

(f1​(z)fn​(z))=M​(e1​(z)en​(z))\pmatrix{f_{1}(z)\cr\vdots\cr f_{n}(z)}=M\pmatrix{e_{1}(z)\cr\vdots\cr e_{n}(z)}

and where (e1​(z),…,en​(z))(e_{1}(z),\ldots,e_{n}(z)) is vector solution of a system of nn homogeneous first order equations with coefficients in ℚ¯​[z,1/z]\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[z,1/z].

2 André’s Theorem and first consequences

Everything we deduce in this paper hinges on the following beautiful Theorem plus Corollary by Yves André.

Theorem 2.1 (Y.André)

Let ff be an EE-function and let L​y=0Ly=0 be its minimal differential equation. Then at every point z≠0,∞z\neq 0,\infty the equation has a basis of holomorphic solutions.

All results that follow now, depend on a limited version of Theorem 2.1 where the EE-function has rational coefficients. Although the following theorem occurs in [A1] we like to give a proof of it to make this paper selfcontained to the extent of only accepting Theorem 2.1.

Corollary 2.2 (Y.André)

Let ff be an EE-function with rational coefficients and let L​y=0Ly=0 be its minimal differential equation. Suppose f⁡(1)=0f(1)=0. Then z=1z=1 is an apparent singularity of L​y=0Ly=0.

Proof Suppose

f⁡(z)=∑n=0∞ann!​zn.f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}{a_{n}\over n!}z^{n}.

Let g⁡(z)=f⁡(z)/(1−z)g(z)=f(z)/(1-z). Note that g⁡(z)g(z) is also holomorphic in ℂ{\mathbb{C}}. Moreover, g⁡(z)g(z) is again an EE-function. Write

g⁡(z)=∑n=0∞bnn!​zng(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}{b_{n}\over n!}z^{n}

where

bnn!=∑k=0nakk!.{b_{n}\over n!}=\sum_{k=0}^{n}{a_{k}\over k!}.

Since f⁡(1)=0f(1)=0 we see that

bnn!=−∑k=n+1∞akk!.{b_{n}\over n!}=-\sum_{k=n+1}^{\infty}{a_{k}\over k!}.

Since ff is an EE-function there exist B,C>0B,C>0 such that |ak|≤B⋅Ck|a_{k}|\leq B\cdot C^{k}. Hence

|bn|\displaystyle|b_{n}| ≤\displaystyle\leq B​n!​|∑k=n∞Ckk!|\displaystyle Bn!\left|\sum_{k=n}^{\infty}{C^{k}\over k!}\right|
≤\displaystyle\leq B​n!​Cnn!​(1+C1!+C22!+⋯)\displaystyle Bn!{C^{n}\over n!}\left(1+{C\over 1!}+{C^{2}\over 2!}+\cdots\right)
≤\displaystyle\leq B​eC⋅Cn\displaystyle Be^{C}\cdot C^{n}

Furthermore, the common denominator of b0,…,bnb_{0},\ldots,b_{n} is bounded above by the common denominator of a0,a1,…,ana_{0},a_{1},\ldots,a_{n}, hence bounded by B1⋅C1nB_{1}\cdot C_{1}^{n} for some B1,C1>0B_{1},C_{1}>0. This shows that f⁡(z)/(z−1)f(z)/(z-1) is an EE-function. The minimal differential operator which annihilates g⁡(z)g(z) is simply L∘(z−1)L\circ(z-1). From André’s theorem 2.1 it follows that the kernel of L∘(z−1)L\circ(z-1) around z=1z=1 is spanned by holomorphic functions. Hence the kernel of LL is spanned by holomorphic solutions times z−1z-1. In other words, all solutions of L​y=0Ly=0 vanish at z=1z=1 and therefore z=1z=1 is an apparent singularity.

qed

Lemma 2.3

Let ff be an EE-function with minimal differential equation L​y=0Ly=0 of order nn. Let GG be its differential galois group and let GoG^{o} be the connected component of the identity in GG. Let VV be the vectorspace spanned by all images of f⁡(z)f(z) under GoG^{o}. Then VV is the complete solution space of L​y=0Ly=0.

Proof The fixed field of GoG^{o} is an algebraic Galois extension KK of ℚ¯​(z)\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(z) with galois group G/GoG/G^{o}. Suppose that VV has dimension mm. Then ff satisfies a linear differential equation with coefficients in KK of order mm. In particular we have a relation

f(m)+pm−1​(z)​f(m−1)+⋯+p1​(z)​f′+p0​(z)​f=0f^{(m)}+p_{m-1}(z)f^{(m-1)}+\cdots+p_{1}(z)f^{\prime}+p_{0}(z)f=0 (1)

for some pi∈Kp_{i}\in K. We subject this relation to analytic continuation. Since ff is an entire function, it has trivial monodromy. By choosing suitable paths we obtain the conjugate relations

f(m)+σ⁡(pm−1)​f(m−1)+⋯+σ⁡(p1)​f′+σ⁡(p0)​f=0f^{(m)}+\sigma(p_{m-1})f^{(m-1)}+\cdots+\sigma(p_{1})f^{\prime}+\sigma(p_{0})f=0

for all σ∈G/Go\sigma\in G/G^{o}. Taking the sum over all these relations gives us a non-trivial differential equation for ff of order mm over ℚ¯​(z)\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(z). From the minimality of L​y=0Ly=0 we now conclude that m=nm=n, i.e. the dimension of VV is nn.

qed

Actually it follows from Theorem 2.1 that the fixed field of GoG^{o} is of the form K=ℚ¯​(z1/r)K=\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(z^{1/r}) for some positive integer rr. But we don’t need that in our proof.

The following Lemma is straightforward consequence of general theory of algebraic groups.

Lemma 2.4

Let G1,…,GrG_{1},\ldots,G_{r} be linear algebraic groups and denote by GioG_{i}^{o} their components of the identity. Let H⊂G1×G2×⋯×GrH\subset G_{1}\times G_{2}\times\cdots\times G_{r} be an algebraic subgroup such that the natural projection πi:H→Gi\pi_{i}:H\to G_{i} is surjective for every ii. Let HoH^{o} be the connected component of the identity in HH. Then the natural projections πi:Ho→Gio\pi_{i}:H^{o}\to G_{i}^{o} are surjective.

Now we prove a generalistaion of André’s Corollary 2.2 to general non-zero algebraic points.

Theorem 2.5

Let ff be an EE-function with minimal differential equation L​y=0Ly=0 of order nn. Suppose that ξ∈ℚ¯∗\xi\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}^{*} and f⁡(ξ)=0f(\xi)=0. Then all solutions of L​yLy vanish at z=ξz=\xi. In particular, L​y=0Ly=0 has an apparent singularity at z=ξz=\xi.

Proof By replacing f⁡(z)f(z) by f⁡(ξ​z)f(\xi z) if necessary, we can assume that ff vanishes at z=1z=1. Let fσ1​(z),…,fσr​(z)f^{\sigma_{1}}(z),\ldots,f^{\sigma_{r}}(z) be the G​a​l​(ℚ¯/ℚ)Gal(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/{\mathbb{Q}})-conjugates of f⁡(z)f(z) where we take fσ1​(z)=f​(z)f^{\sigma_{1}}(z)=f(z). Let Lσi​y=0L^{\sigma_{i}}y=0 be the σi\sigma_{i}-conjugate of L​y=0Ly=0. Note that this is the minimal differential equation satisfied by fσi​(z)f^{\sigma_{i}}(z). Let GiG_{i} be the differential galois group and GioG_{i}^{o} the connected component of the identity. By Lemma 2.3 the images of fσi​(z)f^{\sigma_{i}}(z) under GioG_{i}^{o} span the complete solution space of Lσi​y=0L^{\sigma_{i}}y=0.

The product F⁡(z)=∏i=1rfσi​(z)F(z)=\prod_{i=1}^{r}f^{\sigma_{i}}(z) is an EE-function having rational coefficients. Let ℒ​y=0{\cal L}y=0 be its minimal differential equation. Furthermore, F⁡(1)=0F(1)=0. Hence, from André’s Theorem 2.2 it follows that all solutions of ℒ​y=0{\cal L}y=0 vanish at z=1z=1.

Let HH be the differential galois group of the differential compositum of the Picard-Vessiot extensions corresponding to Lσi​y=0L^{\sigma_{i}}y=0. Note that the image of F⁡(z)F(z) under any h∈Hh\in H is again a solution of ℒ​y=0{\cal L}y=0. In particular this image also vanishes at z=1z=1.

Furthermore, HH is an algebraic subgroup of G1×G2×⋯×GrG_{1}\times G_{2}\times\cdots\times G_{r} such that the natural projections πi:H→Gi\pi_{i}:H\to G_{i} are surjective. Let HoH^{o} be the connected component of the identity of HH. Then, by Lemma 2.4, the projections πi:Ho→Gio\pi_{i}:H^{o}\to G_{i}^{o} are surjective.

Let ViV_{i} be the solution space of local solutions at z=1z=1 of Lσi​y=0L^{\sigma_{i}}y=0. Let WiW_{i} be the linear subspace of solutions vanishing at z=1z=1. The group HoH^{o} acts linearly on each space ViV_{i}. Let vi∈Viv_{i}\in V_{i} be the vector corresponding to the solution fσi​(z)f^{\sigma_{i}}(z). Define Hi={h∈Ho|πi​(h)​vi∈Wi}H_{i}=\{h\in H^{o}|\pi_{i}(h)v_{i}\in W_{i}\}. Then HiH_{i} is a Zariski closed subset of HoH^{o}. Furthermore, because all solutions of ℒ​y=0{\cal L}y=0 vanish at z=1z=1, we have that Ho=∪i=1rHiH^{o}=\cup_{i=1}^{r}H_{i}. Since HoH^{o} is connected this implies that Hi=HoH_{i}=H^{o} for at least one ii. Hence πi​(Hi)=πi​(Ho)=Gio\pi_{i}(H_{i})=\pi_{i}(H^{o})=G_{i}^{o} and we see that g​vi∈Wigv_{i}\in W_{i} for all g∈Giog\in G_{i}^{o}. We conclude that Wi=ViW_{i}=V_{i}. In other words, all local solutions of Lσi​y=0L^{\sigma_{i}}y=0 around z=1z=1 vanish in z=1z=1. By conjugation we now see that the same is true for L​y=0Ly=0.

qed

3 Independence results

We now consider a set of EE-functions f1,…,fnf_{1},\ldots,f_{n} which satisfy a system of homogeneous first order equations

y′=A​yy^{\prime}=Ay

where yy is a vector of unknown functions (y1,…,yn)t(y_{1},\ldots,y_{n})^{t} and AA an n×nn\times n-matrix with entries in ℚ¯​(z)\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(z). The common denominator of these entries is denoted by T⁡(z)T(z).

Lemma 3.1

Let us assume that the ℚ¯​(z)\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(z)-rank of f1,…,fnf_{1},\ldots,f_{n} is mm. Then there is a ℚ¯​[z]\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[z]-basis of relations

Ci,1​(z)​f1​(z)+Ci,2​(z)​f2​(z)+⋯+Ci,n​(z)​fn​(z)≡0i=1,2,…,n−mC_{i,1}(z)f_{1}(z)+C_{i,2}(z)f_{2}(z)+\cdots+C_{i,n}(z)f_{n}(z)\equiv 0\quad i=1,2,\ldots,n-m (2)

such that for any ξ∈ℚ¯\xi\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}} the matrix

(C11​(ξ)C12​(ξ)…C1​n​(ξ)Cn−m,1​(ξ)Cn−m,2​(ξ)…Cn−m,n​(ξ))\pmatrix{C_{11}(\xi)&C_{12}(\xi)&\ldots&C_{1n}(\xi)\cr\vdots&\vdots&&\vdots\cr C_{n-m,1}(\xi)&C_{n-m,2}(\xi)&\ldots&C_{n-m,n}(\xi)\cr}

has rank precisely n−mn-m.

Proof The ℚ¯​(z)\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(z)-dimension of all relations is n−mn-m. Choose an indepent set of n−mn-m relations of the form (2) (without the extra specialisation condition).

Denote the greatest common divisor of the determinants of all (n−m)×(n−m)(n-m)\times(n-m) submatrices of (Ci​j​(z))(C_{ij}(z)) by D⁡(z)D(z). Suppose that D⁡(ξ)=0D(\xi)=0 for some ξ\xi. Then the matrix (Ci​j​(ξ))(C_{ij}(\xi)) has linearly dependent rows. By taking ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}}-linear relations between the rows, if necessary, we can assume that C1​j​(ξ)=0C_{1j}(\xi)=0 for j=1,…,nj=1,\ldots,n. Hence all C1​j​(z)C_{1j}(z) are divisible by z−ξz-\xi and the polynomials C1​j​(z)/(z−ξ)C_{1j}(z)/(z-\xi) are the coefficients of another ℚ¯​(z)\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(z)-linear relation. Replace the first relation by this new relation. The new greatest divisor of all (n−m)×(n−m)(n-m)\times(n-m)-determinants is now D⁡(z)/(z−ξ)D(z)/(z-\xi). By repeating this argument we can find an independent set of n−mn-m relations of the form (2) whose associated D⁡(z)D(z) is a non-zero constant.

But now it is not hard to see that (2) is a ℚ¯​[z]\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[z]-basis of all ℚ¯​[z]\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[z]-relations. Furthermore, D⁡(ξ)≠0D(\xi)\neq 0 for all ξ\xi (because D⁡(z)D(z) is constant), so all specialisations have maximal rank.

qed

Theorem 3.2

Let f1,…,fnf_{1},\ldots,f_{n} be a vector solution of the system

y′=A​yy^{\prime}=Ay

consisting of EE-functions. Let T⁡(z)T(z) be the common denominator of the entries in AA. Then, for any ξ∈ℚ¯\xi\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}, ξ​T​(ξ)≠0\xi T(\xi)\neq 0, any ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}}-linear relation between f1​(ξ),…,fn​(ξ)f_{1}(\xi),\ldots,f_{n}(\xi) arises by specialisation of a ℚ¯​(z)\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(z)-linear relation.

Proof Suppose there exists a ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}}-linear relation

α1​f1​(ξ)+α2​f2​(ξ)+⋯+αn​fn​(ξ)=0\alpha_{1}f_{1}(\xi)+\alpha_{2}f_{2}(\xi)+\cdots+\alpha_{n}f_{n}(\xi)=0

which does not come from specialisation of a ℚ¯​(z)\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(z)-linear relation at z=ξz=\xi. Consider the function

F⁡(z)=A1​(z)​f1​(z)+A2​(z)​f2​(z)+⋯+An​(z)​fn​(z)F(z)=A_{1}(z)f_{1}(z)+A_{2}(z)f_{2}(z)+\cdots+A_{n}(z)f_{n}(z)

where Ai​(z)∈ℚ¯​[z]A_{i}(z)\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[z] to be specified later. Let L​y=0Ly=0 be the minimal differential equation satisfied by FF. Suppose that the ℚ¯​(z)\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(z)-rank of f1,…,fnf_{1},\ldots,f_{n} is mm. It will turn out that the order of L​y=0Ly=0 is at most mm.

We now show how to choose A1​(z),…,An​(z)A_{1}(z),\ldots,A_{n}(z) such that

  1. 1.

    Ai​(ξ)=αiA_{i}(\xi)=\alpha_{i} for i=1,2,…,ni=1,2,\ldots,n

  2. 2.

    The order of L​y=0Ly=0 is mm.

  3. 3.

    ξ\xi is a regular point of L​y=0Ly=0.

By using the system y′=A​yy^{\prime}=Ay recursively we can find Aij​(z)∈ℚ¯​[z]A_{i}^{j}(z)\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[z] such that

F(j)​(z)=∑i=1nAij​(z)​fi​(z).F^{(j)}(z)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}A_{i}^{j}(z)f_{i}(z).

In addition we fix a ℚ¯​(z)\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(z)-basis of linear relations

Ci,1​(z)​f1​(z)+⋯+Ci,n​fn​(z)≡0i=1,…,n−mC_{i,1}(z)f_{1}(z)+\cdots+C_{i,n}f_{n}(z)\equiv 0\quad i=1,\ldots,n-m

with polynomial coefficients Ci​j​(z)C_{ij}(z) such that the (n−m)×n(n-m)\times n-matrix of values Ci​j​(ξ)C_{ij}(\xi) has maximal rank n−mn-m. This is possible in view of Lemma 3.1. Consider the (n+1)×n(n+1)\times n-matrix

ℳ=(C11​(z)…C1​n​(z)Cn−m,1​(z)…Cn−m,n​(z)A1​(z)…An​(z)A1m​(z)…Anm​(z)).{\cal M}=\pmatrix{C_{11}(z)&\ldots&C_{1n}(z)\cr\vdots&&\vdots\cr C_{n-m,1}(z)&\ldots&C_{n-m,n}(z)\cr A_{1}(z)&\ldots&A_{n}(z)\cr\vdots&&\vdots\cr A_{1}^{m}(z)&\ldots&A_{n}^{m}(z)\cr}.

We denote the submatrix obtained from ℳ{\cal M} by deleting the row with Aij​(i=1,…,n)A_{i}^{j}\ (i=1,\ldots,n) by ℳj{\cal M}_{j}. There exists a ℚ¯​(z)\overline{\mathbb{Q}}(z)-linear relation between the rows of ℳ{\cal M} which explains why the minimal equation L​y=0Ly=0 of FF satisfies a differential equation of order ≤m\leq m. This equation has precisely order mm if and only if the submatrix ℳm{\cal M}_{m} has rank mm. In that case the minimal differential equation for FF is given by

Δm​F(m)+…+Δ1​F′+Δ0​F=0\Delta_{m}F^{(m)}+\ldots+\Delta_{1}F^{\prime}+\Delta_{0}F=0

where Δj=(−1)j​det(ℳj)\Delta_{j}=(-1)^{j}\det({\cal M}_{j}).

By induction it is not hard to show that Ai0​(z)=Ai​(z)A_{i}^{0}(z)=A_{i}(z) and

Aij​(z)=Ai(j)+Pi​j​(A1,…,An,…,A1(j−1),…,An(j−1))A_{i}^{j}(z)=A_{i}^{(j)}+P_{ij}(A_{1},\ldots,A_{n},\ldots,A_{1}^{(j-1)},\ldots,A_{n}^{(j-1)})

where

Pi​j∈ℚ¯​[z,1/T⁡(z)]​[X10,…,Xn​0,…,X1,j−1,…,Xn,j−1]P_{ij}\in\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[z,1/T(z)][X_{10},\ldots,X_{n0},\ldots,X_{1,j-1},\ldots,X_{n,j-1}]

are linear forms with coefficients in ℚ¯​[z,1/T​(z)]\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[z,1/T(z)]. We can now choose the Ai​(z)A_{i}(z) and their derivatives in such a way that det(ℳm)\det({\cal M}_{m}) does not vanish in the point ξ\xi. The choice of Ai​(ξ)A_{i}(\xi) is fixed by taking Ai​(ξ)=αiA_{i}(\xi)=\alpha_{i}. Since the relation ∑i=1nαi​fi​(ξ)=0\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{i}f_{i}(\xi)=0 does not come from specialisation, the rows of values (Ci​1​(ξ),…,Ci​n​(ξ))(C_{i1}(\xi),\ldots,C_{in}(\xi)) for i=1,…,n−mi=1,\ldots,n-m and (α1,…,αn)(\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{n}) have maximal rank n−m+1n-m+1. We can now choose the derivates Ai(j)A_{i}^{(j)} recursively with respect to jj such that det(ℳm)​(ξ)≠0\det({\cal M}_{m})(\xi)\neq 0. With this choice we note that conditions (i),(ii),(iii) are satisfied.

On the other hand, F⁡(ξ)=0F(\xi)=0, so it follows from Theorem 2.5 that ξ\xi is a singularity of L​y=0Ly=0. This contradicts condition (iii).

qed

Proof of Theorem 1.3. Consider the vector of EE-functions given by the monomials 𝐟(z)𝐢:=f1(z)i1⋯fn(z)in{\bf f}(z)^{\bf i}:=f_{1}(z)^{i_{1}}\cdots f_{n}(z)^{i_{n}}, i1+…+in=Ni_{1}+\ldots+i_{n}=N of degree NN in f1​(z),…,fn​(z)f_{1}(z),\ldots,f_{n}(z). This vector again satisfies a system of linear first order equations with singularities in the set T⁡(z)=0T(z)=0. So we now apply Theorem 3.2 to the set of EE-functions 𝐟​(z)𝐢{\bf f}(z)^{\bf i}. The relation P⁡(f1​(ξ),…,fn​(ξ))P(f_{1}(\xi),\ldots,f_{n}(\xi)) is now a ℚ¯\overline{\mathbb{Q}}-linear relation between the values 𝐟​(ξ)𝐢{\bf f}(\xi)^{\bf i}. Hence, by Theorem 3.2, there is a ℚ¯​[z]\overline{\mathbb{Q}}[z]-linear relation between the 𝐟​(z)𝐢{\bf f}(z)^{\bf i} which specialises to the linear relation between the values at z=ξz=\xi. This proves our Theorem.

qed

4 Removal of non-zero singularities

In this section we prove Theorem 1.5. For this we require the following Proposition.

Proposition 4.1

Let ff be an EE-function and ξ∈ℚ∗\xi\in{\mathbb{Q}}^{*} such that f⁡(ξ)=0f(\xi)=0. Then f⁡(z)/(z−ξ)f(z)/(z-\xi) is again an EE-function.

Proof By replacing f⁡(z)f(z) by f⁡(ξ​z)f(\xi z) if necessary, we can restrict our attention to ξ=1\xi=1. Write down a basis of local solutions of L​y=0Ly=0 around z=1z=1. Since ff vanishes at z=1z=1, Theorem 2.5 implies that all solutions of L​y=0Ly=0 vanish at z=1z=1. But then, by conjugation, this holds for the solutions around z=1z=1 of the G​a​l​(ℚ¯/ℚ)Gal(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/{\mathbb{Q}})-conjugates Lσ​y=0L^{\sigma}y=0 as well. In particular, the conjugate EE-function fσ​(z)f^{\sigma}(z) vanishes at z=1z=1 for every σ∈G​a​l​(ℚ¯/ℚ)\sigma\in Gal(\overline{\mathbb{Q}}/{\mathbb{Q}}). Taking up the notations of the proof of Theorem 2.2 we now see that

bnσn!=−∑k=n+1∞akσk!{b_{n}^{\sigma}\over n!}=-\sum_{k=n+1}^{\infty}{a_{k}^{\sigma}\over k!}

for every σ\sigma. We can now bound |bnσ||b_{n}^{\sigma}| exponentially in nn for every σ\sigma. Since the coefficients of an EE-function lie in a finite extension of ℚ{\mathbb{Q}}, only finitely many conjugates are involved. So we get our desired bound h⁡(b0,…,bn)=O⁡(n)h(b_{0},\ldots,b_{n})=O(n).

qed

Proof of Theorem 1.5 Denote the column vector (f1​(z),…,fn​(z))t(f_{1}(z),\ldots,f_{n}(z))^{t} by 𝐟⁡(z){\bf f}(z). Let

be the system of equations satisfied by 𝐟{\bf f} and let GG be its differential Galois group. and ℱ1{\cal F}_{1} has entries holomorphic around z=αz=\alpha. Thanks to Proposition 4.1, the entries of the first column in ℱ1{\cal F}_{1} are again EE-functions. Moreover, ℱ1{\cal F}_{1} satisfies the new system of equations

ℱ1′=(D−1​M​A​M−1​D+D−1​D′)​ℱ1.{\cal F}_{1}^{\prime}=(D^{-1}MAM^{-1}D+D^{-1}D^{\prime}){\cal F}_{1}.
